title: How long, O Lord? (Psalm 13)
hookLine: the Bible gives you permission to complain to God

cards: It's two in the morning. The diagnosis hasn't changed. The job hasn't come through.
The person hasn't called back. You've been polite about it for months, and an impolite question is building. Many people assume two options: swallow it, or walk away from God entirely.
The Bible offers a third, in its own prayer book: a psalm that opens with a complaint and doesn't apologize for it.
In the King James words: "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?" That's somebody at the end of their rope, talking straight to God.

teach.b: Lament: a prayer of grief and complaint, spoken to God. You met this psalm on day seventeen, with David shouting at God. Today, the shape is the teaching.
The first two verses ask how long, four times. Then a request: "Consider and hear me, O LORD my God: lighten mine eyes." Look at me.
Answer me. Then the turn: "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation."
Complaint, request, trust. And nothing outside has changed. No answer arrives between verse four and verse five.
The turn happens in the one praying. Scholars count around a third of the Psalms as laments, and some are a whole people's cry, after a defeat or a famine. Not all of them turn; Psalm 88 never does.
Lamentations, a whole book of lament, grieves Jerusalem after the Babylonians burned it, and four of its five chapters are acrostics: each verse starts with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet.
Grief, set out from A to Z. Some readers hear in that a way of saying all of it, every letter, and of giving pain a shape with an end.
You don't complain to someone you think isn't there. A lament keeps talking to God while saying, this hurts, and it isn't right.
Jews have prayed these psalms for many centuries, and on Tisha B'Av, the fast that mourns the temple, Lamentations is chanted aloud. Christians of every church pray the laments too.
For both, honesty isn't the opposite of faith. Sometimes it's what faith sounds like at two in the morning.

how: Christians pray the lament psalms in daily prayer, at funerals and in times of crisis, and many churches hold services of lament after tragedies; some people write their own complaints to God in a journal, following the psalms' shape.

games.q: what's inside the lament — tap the pairs.

s: in Psalm 13, things get better before the psalm turns to trust

Psalm 13 turns to trust. Psalm 88 never turns, and it's still in the Bible.

games.q: you're a poet in Jerusalem after the city has burned. how do you give the grief a shape?
o: a verse for every letter of the alphabet.
write only about the good years before.
games.why: Lamentations sets its grief out letter by letter: four of its five chapters are acrostics. all of it, every letter, said to God.

practice: On paper or your phone, write the thing you've been polite about for too long, in one or two plain sentences. If you pray, start the way the psalm does, how long; if you don't, write it to whoever or whatever you'd want to hear it.
Don't tidy it up or add a happy ending unless one comes; then sit with it.

wordCard.voice: Lament. A prayer of grief and complaint, spoken to God rather than about him.

orig.note: Hebrew: how long? the words that open Psalm 13's complaint, again and again.

carryVoice: Your line: complaint is a prayer too. Tomorrow, when prayer feels empty. Fifteen weeks on the path.
